stories.title: Grandpa Rescued After Kidnap Scare in Malaysia
stories.headline_kid: A 72-year-old Singaporean man was kidnapped by tricksters in Malaysia — but the good news is, he has been rescued safely!
summary: A 72-year-old Singaporean man travelled to Malaysia after being offered a job. Sadly, it was a trap. A group of criminals, called a syndicate, kidnapped him and demanded a huge ransom of S$1 million for his release.
The gang had used social media to first become 'friends' with him online before inviting him to meet in person. This made him trust them, which made it easier for them to trick him.
Thankfully, police in Malaysia's Kedah state managed to track down the kidnappers and rescue the man safely. He was not seriously hurt, and investigations are continuing to catch everyone involved.
This story is a good reminder that job offers from strangers online, especially ones that sound exciting, should always be checked carefully before meeting anyone in person.

lenses.me: If a message or job offer online seems exciting but comes from someone you've never met in real life, always tell a trusted adult before doing anything.
lenses.family: Grandparents and parents can also be targeted by online scams — it helps to talk about these tricks together as a family.
lenses.friends: You and your friends can look out for each other by sharing tips on spotting fake job offers or suspicious messages online.
lenses.nation: Singapore's police work closely with Malaysian police to protect Singaporeans travelling or working abroad.
lenses.world: Kidnap-for-ransom scams happen across many countries, showing why nations need to cooperate to keep people safe.

stories.title: New Rule for Property Agents: Use It or Lose It
stories.headline_kid: Starting 2027, property agents in Singapore must actually help buy or sell homes regularly — or they could lose their licence to work.
summary: In Singapore, people who help others buy, sell or rent homes are called property agents. Soon, there will be a new rule: agents must complete at least three transactions (deals) every three years, or pass a special test, to keep their licence.
This rule is meant to make sure agents stay sharp and know what they are doing, since buying a home is one of the biggest decisions a family can make.

However, some news reports say a few agents might try to 'borrow' transactions — meaning they let their name appear on a deal they didn't really work on, just to meet the requirement. This goes against the spirit of the rule.
Authorities are watching closely to make sure agents follow the rules properly, so that families can trust the person helping them with such an important decision.

lenses.me: If your family ever buys or sells a home, you'll want a serious, experienced agent helping — not someone just ticking a box.
lenses.family: Parents can ask questions about an agent's experience before trusting them with something as important as a home.
lenses.friends: You could chat with friends about their family's HDB flat and how their parents chose an agent.
lenses.nation: This rule helps keep Singapore's property market fair and trustworthy for everyone.
lenses.world: Many countries face similar challenges making sure professionals stay qualified and honest in their jobs.

stories.title: Nine Days of Rain Bring Disaster to the Philippines
stories.headline_kid: Nine days of non-stop rain have caused terrible floods and landslides in the Philippines, sadly killing at least 16 people.
summary: For nine days straight, heavy rain — made worse by tropical storms — has been pouring down on the Philippines' main island, Luzon. In some places, more rain fell than usually falls in an entire month!

The rain caused floods in the streets of the capital city, Manila, and landslides in the hilly city of Baguio, where a mountainside collapsed onto several homes. At least 16 people have died, and rescuers are still searching through the rubble for survivors.
Because of the danger, schools and government offices across Luzon have been closed. Many families have had to leave their homes to stay somewhere safer.
This disaster shows how quickly heavy rain can turn dangerous, especially in areas with hills or crowded cities. Rescue teams are working hard to help everyone affected.

lenses.me: Even here in Singapore, when it rains very heavily, it's important to stay away from flooded drains and slopes.
lenses.family: If your family is planning a trip to the Philippines, it's wise to check the weather news first.
lenses.friends: Some classmates might have relatives in the Philippines — it's kind to check in on how they're doing.
lenses.nation: Singapore sometimes sends help, like rescue teams or supplies, to neighbouring countries during big disasters.
lenses.world: Scientists say heavier and longer rainstorms may become more common as our climate changes.

stories.title: Should Roblox Be Banned to Keep Kids Safe Online?
stories.headline_kid: Some countries want to ban the popular game Roblox to protect children online — but experts say banning apps may not solve the real problem.
summary: Roblox is a hugely popular online game where players can build and play thousands of mini-games. But some governments are worried that harmful content or dangerous strangers could reach children through such platforms, especially after cases linked to online radicalisation — where people are influenced to believe harmful or extreme ideas.

A few countries have already banned Roblox, hoping this will protect children. But an online safety expert says banning the app doesn't automatically make children safer, since most of what happens on Roblox has nothing to do with extremism at all.
Instead, experts suggest better solutions: stronger safety settings on the app itself, more counselling and support for children, and parents staying involved in what their kids do online.
This shows that keeping children safe online isn't just about blocking one app — it's about teaching kids to recognise danger and making sure trusted adults are part of the conversation.

lenses.me: If something feels wrong or scary while gaming online, always tell a trusted adult right away.
lenses.family: Parents and children can talk together about which games are okay and set sensible screen time limits.
lenses.friends: You and your friends can look out for each other and report anything unsafe you see while playing together.
lenses.nation: Singapore focuses on teaching digital literacy in schools so children learn to spot online dangers themselves.
lenses.world: Different countries are trying different ways to protect children online, showing there's no single perfect solution yet.

stories.title: A Samurai's Home Turned Into a Magical Hotel
stories.headline_kid: In Japan, an old samurai family's mansion has become a stunning hotel called Ohana Ryokan, complete with a 200-year-old pine garden.
summary: In Yanagawa, a town near Fukuoka in Japan, there's a special place called Ohana Ryokan. It used to be the home of the Tachibana family, who were once samurai — Japan's famous warrior class from long ago.

The estate survived difficult times after World War II and has now become a hotel where guests can sleep in historic rooms and walk through the Shoto-en Garden, home to about 150 pine trees, some over 200 years old!

Ohana is so beautiful that it has been officially named a 'Place of Scenic Beauty' by Japan — the same special honour given to famous spots like Mount Fuji and the Arashiyama Bamboo Grove in Kyoto. In fact, Ohana is the only hotel in Japan where guests can actually stay overnight inside such a special protected place.
Japan is one of the most popular holiday destinations for Singaporean families, so a trip to a historic place like this could be an unforgettable adventure — a real walk back in time.

lenses.me: Imagine sleeping in a house where samurai warriors once lived hundreds of years ago — what would you want to explore first?
lenses.family: Japan is a favourite holiday spot for many Singapore families; this could be a unique place to add to a future trip.
lenses.friends: You could share fun facts about samurai history with friends who love Japanese culture or anime.
lenses.nation: Many Singaporeans travel to Japan every year, which helps build strong cultural and travel ties between the two countries.
lenses.world: Turning old historic buildings into hotels helps keep important history alive for future generations to enjoy.
